## Week 1 — What kind of problem, and how wrong is the fit

### Lecture 1 — Ontology and error

**Async.** Where AIML shows up in engineering (digital twins, activity
classification, segmentation). The family tree: supervised, unsupervised,
self-supervised, reinforcement; under those, classification, regression,
clustering, dimensionality reduction, and names the course only points at
(active learning, transfer learning, contrastive learning, semi-supervised
learning, physics-informed nets, GANs, policy learning, actor-critic). The
supervised goal is a function from features to a label. Vector norms. Error
as MSE and as MAE, and why the choice of error changes what "close" means.

**Sync.** Course shape (async lecture, then sync hour, then homework). A
second pass on the ontology, the playground network, the norms, and MSE
versus MAE.

### Lecture 2 — Gradient descent and nearest neighbors

**Async.** Gradient descent: step against the gradient, and what changes when
the function is no longer a function of one scalar. k-NN classification: the
label is a vote of the $k$ nearest training points. k-NN regression: the
prediction is an average of those neighbors. Distance, the choice of $k$, and
the cost of keeping the whole training set.

**Sync.** Reproducibility (a random seed). Ground truth versus a noisy
sample, and the normal curve as the picture of that noise. A linear
regression picture before week 2. Gradient descent uses only first-derivative
information.

## Week 2 — Linear least squares

### Lecture 1 — The closed form

**Async.** Nomenclature: features, parameters, prediction, residual. The
approach: pick a model (a line, or a polynomial), stack every sample into a
design matrix, write the squared-error objective, and solve. The normal
equations. A trained model is the parameter vector. Model bias: a form that
cannot express the data, no matter the parameters. Least squares with two
input features.

**Sync.** A linear *function* and linear *regression* are different claims.
Walking a cubic model all the way to $Xw \approx y$, and the tall-skinny
shape of $X$. Same training steps for a different basis. Choosing complexity.
NumPy arrays, vectors, matrices, and broadcasting.

### Lecture 2 — Iterative solvers and regularization

**Async.** Gradient descent on the least-squares loss, for when the closed
form is a bad idea. Full-batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent,
and mini-batch. $L_2$ regularization: penalize large weights so a high-order
fit stays smooth. Other penalties exist; $L_2$ is the one derived here.

**Sync.** Why the closed form breaks (cost, conditioning). Least squares is
convex, so gradient descent is chasing a global minimum. Feature scale
changes the path the steps take. A side-by-side of the three gradient
methods. Complexity wins an unregularized fit and then fails on new points.
Which solver to reach for.

## Week 3 — Logistic regression

Hand derivation: [logistic regression](../logistic-regression/index.qmd).

### Lecture 1 — Binary

**Async.** Least squares is a poor classifier: the target is a category, and
a line unbounded in $y$ is hard to tame. The sigmoid squashes the linear
score into $(0, 1)$. A linear score gives a linear decision boundary;
expanded features bend it. Training is maximum likelihood, which becomes a
loss to descend. $L_2$ again, through the parameter $C$. Predicting is a
threshold on the probability.

**Sync.** The probability reading of the sigmoid. Who-ate-the-pie as the
likelihood story. The train step and the predict step written as a pair.
A coding pass, and a short side trip through a multivariate Gaussian.

### Lecture 2 — More than two classes

**Async.** One-versus-one: a binary model for every pair, then a vote.
Multinomial logistic regression: one weight vector per class. One-hot
labels. Cross-entropy, and the batch version; it is zero when the predicted
distribution matches the label. Softmax turns the class scores into a
distribution. Odds ratios.

**Sync.** One-versus-all (one-versus-rest) beside one-versus-one, and what
each is approximating. Odds for one class, then the full distribution.
Training and prediction for the multinomial model.

## Week 4 — Support vector machines

Hand derivation: [support vector machines](../support-vector-machine/index.qmd).

### Lecture 1 — Max margin, then a soft margin

**Async.** A linear discriminant, and why the large-margin one is the one to
keep. The margin as a constrained quadratic program. Support vectors are the
training points that sit on the margin and determine the boundary. The dual,
via Lagrange multipliers, is how those points are found. A soft margin lets
some points cross, with a penalty.

**Sync.** Hard-margin training restated as quadratic programming in standard
form. The Lagrangian and the dual, with the Mario Kart picture for staying
inside the constraints. What the trained machine stores. Notes on using the
result.

### Lecture 2 — Kernels, several classes, regression

**Async.** A feature map makes a nonlinear boundary linear in a new space.
The kernel trick evaluates inner products there without building the map.
The same quadratic program, with the kernel in place. Multi-class SVM by
reducing to binary problems. Support vector regression.

**Sync.** Hard margin fails when the classes overlap; slack variables and $C$.
A 1-D example that separates only after the features grow. Mercer's
condition: which functions are legal kernels. The sklearn set: linear,
polynomial, RBF, sigmoid. RBF corresponds to an infinite polynomial feature
map with decaying weights. How a kernel model is evaluated on a new point.
$\varepsilon$-insensitive loss: SVR ignores errors inside a tube, then pays
for the rest. Soft-margin SVR.

## Week 5 — Decision trees and forests

### Lecture 1 — Classification trees

**Async.** A tree is a stack of binary questions. Features may be numeric or
categorical, and some values may be missing. Gini impurity measures how mixed
a node is; the split that most reduces it is the one taken. Top-down
induction. Continuous features are split at a threshold. Deeper trees cut the
space into smaller boxes. Reading a leaf to predict. Hyperparameters that
limit depth. Feature expansion still applies in front of a tree.

**Sync.** Gini of a candidate split, worked on a small table. The same depth
story. Regularizing with those hyperparameters. White box versus black box:
a tree can be read. How a missing value can still be routed.

### Lecture 2 — Regression trees, bagging, random forests

**Async.** A regression tree predicts a constant on each leaf; the split
minimizes a squared-error cost. Shallow versus deep, and what happens out of
the range of the training values. Bootstrap aggregation: many trees on
bootstrap samples, then average. A random forest also randomizes which
features each split may see. Comparison with one tree.

**Sync.** The regression cost, and pictures of a shallow tree, a deep tree,
and two out-of-sample cases. Ensemble learning as a crowd of weak, diverse
trees. Bootstrap sampling drawn out on a smaller example. The forest as
bagging plus feature randomness.

## Week 6 — Feature engineering

### Lecture 1 — Scaling and transforms

**Async.** Columns on different scales (the California housing example:
income versus occupancy) distort distance and the size of a gradient step.
Min–max normalization. Standardization to zero mean and unit variance. Log
transform. Power transforms: Box–Cox and Yeo–Johnson. Quantile transform
toward a uniform or a normal distribution. Fit the transform on the training
rows, then apply that same map to anything new.

**Sync.** Why scale shows up in distance, in which feature dominates a linear
model, and in training. The same gallery of scalers, with the nonlinear ones
separated from min–max and standard. A coding pass.

### Lecture 2 — Which columns to keep

**Async.** Filter methods score a column without training the final model.
Pearson correlation: drop one of two features that move together, keeping
the one more tied to the target. Variance inflation factor: how well a
feature is already a linear combination of the others, via $R^2$. Wrapper
methods train a model inside the search. Recursive feature elimination drops
the weakest column and refits. Feature importance after a fit. Feature
expansion is the opposite move: add columns. Selection and dimensionality
reduction answer different questions.

**Sync.** A second pass on the Pearson procedure and on VIF, then wrappers
and RFE. The selection-versus-reduction note is the one to reread before
week 12.

## Week 7 — Neural networks, the forward picture

Deeper notes: [neural networks](../neural-networks/index.qmd).

### Lecture 1 — From a perceptron to a stack of layers

**Async.** A network can do regression, including several outputs, and
nonlinear classification. Shallow versus deep: a small net has tens of
weights; AlexNet-scale models have tens of millions. This course trains the
shallow ones. "Data hungry" is about big nets; a few parameters do not
require a huge sample. The key move is minimizing a loss by backpropagation.
A network generalizes logistic regression, and one hidden layer is a
universal approximator. Biology supplies the picture: a node is a neuron, a
weight is a synapse, and the node applies an activation. A perceptron is a
weighted sum of inputs, plus a bias, then an activation (the worked example
uses a sigmoid). Layers: input, hidden, output. Training adjusts the weight
matrices so the output matches the labels; regression uses MSE and gradient
descent. Forward propagation sends one sample through at a time. In matrix
form, $W$ is shaped so that it maps the incoming width to the outgoing
width; entry $W_{i,j}$ connects source $j$ to target $i$. Softmax on the
output makes the class scores sum to 1, the same device as multinomial
logistic regression. A bias is an extra input fixed at 1, so a layer with
$n$ inputs and $m$ outputs has $(n+1) \times m$ trainable weights. In
PyTorch the bias is a flag, on by default; the library inserts it.

**Sync.** One perceptron cannot separate data that is not linearly
separable; XOR is the example, and that limit is tied to the first AI
winter. The learning step is named as backward propagation plus a gradient
update. The rest of the hour walks the async lecture again: the ontology,
the forward pass, the matrix form, softmax, and the parameter count.

### Lecture 2 — Activation functions

**Async.** A node applies a nonlinearity; without it, a stack of layers is
still one linear map. Sigmoid, and the steepness that approaches a step.
Tanh. The identity. Softmax, as a distribution over classes rather than a
hidden-unit activation. ReLU and leaky ReLU. Vanishing gradients: a
saturated sigmoid or tanh sends almost no signal backward. A comparison
table of advantages and failure modes.

**Sync.** The same functions, plus ELU and GELU. How to choose: hidden units
versus the output unit, regression versus classification. A forward-pass
coding example.

## Week 8 — Training a network

### Lecture 1 — Backpropagation

**Async.** The loss depends on a weight through every layer above it.
Backpropagation is the chain rule organized from the output backward: one
layer, then several, first with scalars and no bias. The training summary:
forward, loss, backward, step. Learning curves. Underfitting versus
overfitting as shapes of those curves. Batch, iteration, and epoch.
Learning rate, momentum, and Adam. Regularization.

**Sync.** Why the gradient is the expensive object, and what else has to be
known to say how a parameter moves the loss. The delta rule. The same
training summary, then notes on the practical knobs.

### Lecture 2 — PyTorch

**Async.** Tensors as NumPy with a device and a gradient. `torch.nn.Module`
and a small `Sequential` net. A regression head versus a classification head.
An optimizer, the training loop (zero the grads, forward, loss, backward,
step), a learning-rate scheduler, the loss curve, and a validation pass
inside training. `Dataset` and `DataLoader` for batched data.

**Sync.** Stochastic, full-batch, and mini-batch updates again, now on the
network loss surface. Iteration versus epoch. Learning rate, momentum, Adam.
Underfit, overfit, regularization. Then the same PyTorch objects as the
async deck.

## Week 9 — Metrics

### Lecture 1 — Regression

**Async.** MAE ($L_1$), MSE ($L_2$), Huber (quadratic near zero, linear in
the tails), MAPE (error as a fraction of the true value). $R^2$ as the
fraction of variance the model captures, adjusted $R^2$ so extra features
do not inflate it, and a plot of predicted versus true. $R^2$ is not the
Pearson correlation: correlation ignores slope and intercept. sklearn's
metric functions.

**Sync.** A metric itself has a bias; the model will chase whatever is
written down. The same list, with the "is this model good?" check next to
MSE, and the correlation-versus-$R^2$ distinction drawn out. Adjusted $R^2$
uses the feature count, not counting the bias term.

### Lecture 2 — Classification

**Async.** The confusion matrix: true positive, false positive, true
negative, false negative. Accuracy, and why a skewed class makes it look
kind. Precision (of the predicted positives, how many are real). Recall (of
the real positives, how many were found). F1 as the balance of those two.
ROC and AUC are flagged as further reading. The same matrix for more than
two classes; a good model is dark on the diagonal. sklearn's display.

**Sync.** The four cells told as engineering cases (a miss and a false alarm
cost different things). Precision alone and recall alone each hide a
failure. A worked F1 example. Multi-class matrices again.

## Week 10 — Bias, variance, and honest evaluation

The working version of the splits is in the
[workflow](../ml-workflow/index.qmd).

### Lecture 1 — Bias–variance

**Async.** Bias: the model class cannot represent the target (high bias
looks underfit and stable). Variance: the fit swings when the training
sample changes (high variance looks overfit). The tradeoff as model
complexity grows. How to recognize each from training versus held-out
behavior.

**Sync.** Mean and variance as moments of a density, so the names match the
statistics. Three sources of error: bias, variance, and noise in the
response. The same inputs can give different outputs. Performance moves when
the sample moves. Detecting high variance and high bias in practice.

### Lecture 2 — Model selection

**Async.** Hold out a test set for a last estimate. Inside the rest, a
validation set for choices: depth, learning rate, regularization weight,
which features, how many layers. The simple approach is one split. The
rigorous approach is k-fold: every training point takes a turn being the
held-out fold, and the score is the average. Use that average to select.
sklearn estimators share `fit` / `predict`, which is why one loop can try
many models.

**Sync.** The simple split drawn as train / validation / test. K-fold on a
classifier, on a regressor, for selection, and for a final assessment. When
k-fold is worth the cost. A boxplot of fold scores.

## Week 11 — Unsupervised learning and clustering

### Lecture 1 — k-means and hierarchical clustering

**Async.** Unsupervised: there is no label to match. Clustering asks how
many groups, and what counts as a group. There is no single best algorithm;
scale the features first or the units choose the clusters. k-means: assign
to the nearest center, recompute centers, repeat. Initialization matters.
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges; a dendrogram is the
picture; a cut of the tree is a flat clustering.

**Sync.** Centroid methods versus others. k-means factors, including the
shape of the cloud it assumes. Linkage: single (closest pair of members),
complete (farthest pair), average (centroids). The curse of dimensionality
as distances get less informative.

### Lecture 2 — How many clusters, and other algorithms

**Async.** Inertia, and the elbow: more clusters always lower it, so the
bend is the candidate. Silhouette: how well a point sits in its cluster
versus the next one. Spectral clustering: a graph of the points, then
clusters in a space of eigenvectors, which can follow non-convex shapes.
Gaussian mixture models: each cluster is a Gaussian, and a point has a
soft membership. DBSCAN: dense regions separated by sparse ones; `eps` and
`min_samples`. A comparison figure of the sklearn clusterers on the same
shapes.

**Sync.** Inertia as the k-means objective, and why chasing the smallest
inertia just grows $k$. The elbow and the silhouette drawn again. Spectral
clustering told through vibration modes: the graph, its spectrum, clustering
in that spectrum. GMM with too many components versus a coarser fit. DBSCAN's
density rule.

## Week 12 — Dimensionality reduction

### Lecture 1 — PCA

**Async.** A smaller set of coordinates that still carries the spread.
PCA: orthogonal directions from the covariance, ordered by variance.
Center the data (the mean vector). Encoding is projection onto those
directions. Decoding with every component is lossless for the training span;
keeping a prefix is a lossy reconstruction. How many components: cumulative
explained variance. The recipe, and sklearn's `PCA`.

**Sync.** One coordinate for a 2-D cloud, as the motivation. Covariance as
the object that holds spread and correlation. Principal axes on examples,
including a 3-D and a 5-D case. Encoding and decoding as a shift plus a
rotation. Lossy reconstruction again.

### Lecture 2 — Many more features than samples, and nonlinear maps

**Async.** When the dimension exceeds the number of samples, the covariance
is rank deficient; the recipe changes, and at most $n$ components are real.
Eigenfaces: the mean face, the principal faces, a 2-D projection, and
reconstructions as more components return. PCA from scratch and through
sklearn, including on a signed-distance-field set. Linear maps versus
nonlinear ones: locally linear embedding, Isomap, autoencoders. t-SNE for a
2-D or 3-D picture of a high-dimensional set; perplexity is the neighborhood
size. t-SNE is a visualization method.

**Sync.** The rank-deficient case and the eigenface sequence again, with the
projection drawn in more steps. The same nonlinear gallery and the same
perplexity note.

## Week 13 — Ensembles

### Lecture 1 — Bagging and stacking

**Async.** Bootstrapping is sampling with replacement. Bagging averages
models trained on those samples (or votes, for labels). A random forest is
bagging plus a random subset of features at each split. sklearn bagging for
regression and for classification. Stacking: the base models' predictions
become the features of a second model.

**Sync.** An ensemble wants weak learners that are diverse and not bad;
identical models do not average into anything new. Pasting is sampling
without replacement, next to the bootstrap. Bagging versus stacking: one
combines by a fixed vote, the other learns the combination.

### Lecture 2 — Boosting

**Async.** Boosting adds models in sequence, each one aimed at the residual
of the ensemble so far. Gradient boosting: fit a tree to the negative
gradient of the loss. Shrinkage is the learning rate on each new tree.
sklearn's gradient boosting. XGBoost: a regularized objective, a greedy
search for the next tree, and weights on the leaves.

**Sync.** Gradient boosted regression trees, step by step, including the
view that ignores $x$ and treats the prediction as the variable being
updated. Shrinkage again. How XGBoost picks the next tree, and how that
differs from plain gradient boosting.

## Week 14 — Deep learning, as a map

### Lecture 1 — Families, and the edge of the course

**Async.** A survey, not a working treatment. Convolutional nets for images.
Recurrent nets for sequences. Autoencoders and variational autoencoders.
GANs. Graph neural nets. Attention. Diffusion models. Transformers and large
language models.

**Sync.** AI, machine learning, and deep learning as nested ideas, with the
Samuel and Mitchell definitions. "Deep" is a moving word: more than two
hidden layers once counted. Depth as another way to grow capacity, beside
width. Inductive bias: the architecture should match the data. Convolution
and learnable kernels; the Hubel and Wiesel picture for images. Recurrence
for sequences. Attention as a weighted look at other positions, and
transformers built on it. Graphs and message passing. Deep generative
modeling: a VAE learns a distribution in a latent space; a GAN pits a
generator against a discriminator; diffusion iteratively denoises.

The sync hour also marks what this course only named or skipped, so I do not
confuse a mention with a method I can apply: Gaussian processes, Bayesian
optimization, active learning, Bayesian networks, Markov decision processes,
uncertainty quantification, variational inference, reinforcement learning,
model predictive control, causality, physics-informed nets and neural
operators, normalizing flows and energy-based models, and language-model
work beyond the transformer slide. The ontology slide in that hour is the
one that separates "covered in detail" from "brief introduction."
